summary.title: Service Reliability Mathematics
summary.one_liner: Uptime percentages hide important nuances: downtime timing, failure correlation, measurement error, and the rising cost of each additional nine.
takeaways: 99.9% uptime allows about 8h 46m of downtime per year, but one long outage and many short ones with the same total have very different impact.
Each extra nine usually needs a large jump in architecture and operational effort, from single-region failover to multi-region, active-active, and chaos engineering.
The independence and uniform-failure assumptions behind simple uptime math often fail because failures cluster and cascade.
At high availability levels, measurement error can exceed the downtime being measured, so monitoring quality matters.
Modern reliability practice favors error budgets, SLOs per customer tier or feature, and user-experience metrics over a single uptime percentage.
summary.summary: The article argues that a single uptime percentage is an oversimplified way to describe service reliability. It walks through the downtime implied by 99.9% to 99.9999% availability and explains how the architecture needed for each additional nine grows in complexity and cost. It then lists hidden assumptions in naive availability math, such as independent and uniformly distributed failures, and discusses trade-offs, measurement accuracy, human factors, and newer metrics like error budgets and SLOs. It is a conceptual essay with bulleted lists rather than a hands-on tutorial.
